artworks.title: The Tortoise Trainer
artworks.image_credit: Public domain; Wikimedia Commons, 'Osman Hamdi Bey - The Tortoise Trainer - Google Art Project.jpg'

core.text: The Tortoise Trainer is an oil painting from 1906 by Osman Hamdi Bey, an Ottoman painter and archaeologist.
core.source: Wikipedia 'The Tortoise Trainer'; Pera Museum collection record

core.text: An elderly man in a long red robe and a turban holds a ney flute, with a nakkare drum on his back, and tries to train five tortoises.
core.source: Aslan 2014, p. 118 (via Wikipedia); Pera Museum description

detail.text: The scene is set in a worn upper room of the Green Mosque in Bursa. The inscription above the window reads: the healing of the hearts is meeting with the beloved.
The painting is usually read as satire on the slow and ineffective attempts to reform the Ottoman Empire.
detail.source: Wikipedia lead (uncited there); Pera Museum context text. Verify before the study.

detail.text: This 1906 version hangs in the Pera Museum in Istanbul. Osman Hamdi Bey painted a second version in 1907.
detail.source: Pera Museum / Google Arts & Culture; Wikipedia 'Versions'

recall.q: Who painted The Tortoise Trainer, and in which year?
Which instrument does the man hold in his hands?
How many tortoises is the man training?
In which building is the scene set?
In which museum is the 1906 version today?
Why might a viewer read a man patiently training very slow tortoises as a comment on his time?
recall.a: it can be read as satire on slow, ineffective reform (change that does not move)

prior_knowledge.label: I already know where the scene is set
I already know how the painting is usually interpreted
I already know which museum holds it

artworks.title: Portrait of Sultan Mehmed II
artworks.image_credit: Public domain; Wikimedia Commons, 'Bellini, Gentile - Portrait of Mehmed II - National Gallery, London.jpg'
artworks.status: checked against secondary sources (11 Nov 2026); visual description in c2 to verify

core.text: This portrait of Sultan Mehmed II, the Ottoman ruler who conquered Constantinople, is dated 1480 and attributed to the Venetian painter Gentile Bellini.
core.source: National Gallery NG3099 record; Wikipedia 'Portrait of Mehmet II'

core.text: The sultan is shown in profile, framed by a stone arch, with an embroidered cloth hanging over the ledge in front of him.
core.source: Visual description; verify against the National Gallery page

detail.text: Bellini went to Istanbul after Venice and the Ottomans made peace in 1479, when the sultan asked Venice to send a good painter.
Much of the paint was redone in the nineteenth century, especially the figure, so it is debated how much is Bellini's own work.
An old inscription at the lower right gives the date 25 November 1480. The portrait is in the National Gallery in London.
detail.source: Wikimedia file page quoting the National Gallery

recall.q: Which sultan does the portrait show?
In which year is the portrait dated?
Why can we not be sure how the portrait looked when Bellini finished it?
recall.a: it was largely repainted in the 19th century

artworks.title: Ambassador Cornelis Calkoen at his Audience with Sultan Ahmed III
artworks.image_credit: Public domain; Rijksmuseum SK-A-4078 via Wikimedia Commons
artworks.status: checked against secondary sources (11 Nov 2026); visual description in c2 to verify

core.text: Jean-Baptiste Vanmour painted the Dutch ambassador Cornelis Calkoen being received by Sultan Ahmed III in Istanbul on 14 September 1727.
core.source: Rijksmuseum SK-A-4078 title; Wikipedia 'Jean Baptiste Vanmour'

core.text: The sultan sits on his throne in the palace while the ambassador and his party stand before him.
core.source: Visual description; verify against the Rijksmuseum page

detail.text: Vanmour, born in Valenciennes in 1671, came to Istanbul in 1699 with the French ambassador, and audiences with the sultan became his speciality.
Calkoen asked Vanmour to record his audience. Vanmour knew the court ceremony because he could enter the palace with an ambassador's retinue.
Calkoen took the paintings home; they passed through Amsterdam institutions, were reunited in 1903 and hang together in the Rijksmuseum.

recall.q: Which sultan received the ambassador?
Which country did the ambassador represent?
Why could Vanmour show the ceremony so accurately?
recall.a: he entered the palace with ambassadors' retinues and knew the protocol

artworks.title: The Starry Night
artworks.image_credit: Public domain; Google Art Project via Wikimedia Commons

core.text: Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night in June 1889 while staying at the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence.
It shows the view from his east-facing window just before sunrise: a swirling sky, a crescent moon and a tall cypress tree in the foreground.

detail.text: The brightest star, just to the right of the cypress, is thought to be Venus, which was visible at dawn in Provence that spring.
The village could not be seen from his window. Van Gogh added it from a sketch he had made on a hillside above Saint-Rémy.
The Museum of Modern Art in New York acquired the painting in 1941 through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest.

recall.q: Where was Van Gogh staying when he painted it?
Which tall tree stands in the foreground?
Why is the painting not an exact picture of the view from his window?
recall.a: he added the village from another sketch

artworks.title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
artworks.image_credit: CC0; Metropolitan Museum of Art (DP141042) via Wikimedia Commons

core.text: The Great Wave off Kanagawa is a woodblock print by Katsushika Hokusai, the first print of his series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, designed around 1831.
core.source: Wikipedia 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa' (British Museum)

core.text: A huge wave curls over three boats full of rowers, while snow-capped Mount Fuji appears in the background.

detail.text: It was among the first Japanese prints to use Prussian blue, a pigment imported through the Dutch and widely used from 1829.
The boats are fast barges that carried live fish to the markets of Edo; each has eight rowers.
About a thousand copies were printed at first. This impression belongs to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

recall.q: Which mountain appears in the background?
How many boats are under the wave?
Why did the blue of this print look new to buyers at the time?

artworks.title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
artworks.image_credit: Public domain; Mauritshuis via Wikimedia Commons

core.text: Johannes Vermeer painted Girl with a Pearl Earring around 1665, in oil on canvas.
A girl in an oriental turban looks over her shoulder at the viewer, with a large pearl hanging from her ear.

detail.text: It is a tronie, a Dutch picture of a head or a character type, not a portrait of a known person.
A 2018 research project found delicate eyelashes and a green curtain behind the girl that can no longer be seen.
A collector bought it at auction in 1881 for two guilders and thirty cents; it came to the Mauritshuis in The Hague by bequest in 1902.

recall.q: What does the girl wear on her head?
Around which year was it painted?
Why does nobody know who the girl was?
recall.a: it is a tronie, a character study rather than a portrait

artworks.title: The Hunters in the Snow
artworks.image_credit: Public domain; Google Art Project via Wikimedia Commons

core.text: Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted The Hunters in the Snow in 1565, in oil on a wooden panel.
Three tired hunters with their dogs come back through the snow carrying only a fox, while people skate on the frozen ponds below.

detail.text: It belongs to a series about the times of the year; five of these paintings survive.
The inn sign reads 'This is the Golden Hart' and shows a saint linked to hunters, Hubertus or Eustace.
It hangs in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna and was painted as a run of very harsh winters, linked to the Little Ice Age, began.

recall.q: Which season does the painting show?
How many hunters are coming back?
What in the scene suggests that the hunt did not go well?
recall.a: they carry only a fox and look tired
